review.title: Give a scheduled export its own context

brief.problem: Scheduled exports run with whatever tenant the last web request left in a request-scoped singleton, and they skip the filters a web export goes through. Two incidents have been patched by clearing the slot; the mechanism is unchanged. The ticket asks for an export to carry its own context and for both paths to share one filter chain.

options.title: Clear the slot between jobs and pin the incidents with tests
options.argument_for: Smallest change, and both incidents get a regression test.
options.argument_against: Leaves an export able to run with another tenant's context after the next new entry point.

verdicts.why: The two known incidents stop recurring; the slot is still writable by the web middleware.
The builder keeps asking whether a request is in flight.
The scheduled path still builds its own query.

options.title: Give the export its own context object, keep the shared builder
options.argument_for: One owned object the web cannot overwrite, and a small diff in the worker.
options.argument_against: The builder keeps its branch, so a third entry point learns the branch again.

verdicts.why: A context constructed by the caller cannot be overwritten by a request.
The builder still branches, but once, through a named accessor.
The filters are untouched.

options.title: An export context passed explicitly, and one filter chain for both
options.argument_for: Fixes all three: owned context, no branch in the builder, one filter chain.
options.argument_against: Two entry points to keep in step, and the filter chain has to be callable from outside the web path first.

verdicts.why: The context is an argument through the whole path.
The builder asks its context and has no branch left.
One filter chain serves both entry points.

options.title: A tenant-scoped database connection per export
options.argument_for: No shared state to overwrite, because the connection carries the tenant.
options.argument_against: A connection per tenant per export is a pool size nobody has measured, and it fixes nothing about the filters.

options.title: Make the scheduled path call the web path's controller
options.argument_for: The filters are reused without being moved anywhere.
options.argument_against: A job driving a controller needs a fabricated request, which is the ambient state this is meant to remove.

verdicts.why: The tenant still arrives through ambient state.
The branch is where it was.
The scheduled path is made to call the web path's filters.

options.title: Extract reporting into a service with its own entry points
options.argument_for: Everything the report needs becomes an argument, and the web is one caller of many.
options.argument_against: The largest change of the eight, and the audit entry needs a product answer before it can move.

verdicts.why: Nothing reads the slot once the export is a separate service.
The builder is given everything it needs.
The filters move with it, but the audit entry needs a second decision.

options.title: Carry the tenant in a signed manifest the schedule writes
options.argument_for: The tenant travels with the work rather than being looked up when the work runs.
options.argument_against: A manifest is a second format to version, and it answers nothing about the filters.

The builder reads the manifest rather than the request.

verdicts.why: A tenant-per-connection pool means no slot to overwrite.
The builder's branch is unaffected.

brief.headline: Scheduled exports get their own context, so the report builder no longer reads whichever tenant a web request left behind.
brief.how_it_works_today: Every report is built by one class. For a web export it reads the tenant from a request-scoped singleton the middleware wrote, applies a row-visibility filter, a column policy and a redaction pass, and writes the file to a bucket resolved from that same singleton. For a scheduled export there is no request, so the queued job sets the singleton itself and the builder takes a different branch that goes straight from the report definition to the query.

brief.flow_after_caption: The export carries its own context, and both paths share one chain

blind_pass.given:
A multi-tenant PHP web application serves reports. A signed-in person opens a report and exports it; the export runs inside their request, and the tenant they belong to is resolved by middleware into a request-scoped singleton that the report builder reads.

The same application also runs scheduled exports. A nightly command dispatches a queued job per schedule. There is no request and nobody signed in, so the job sets the same singleton itself before building the report.

How it works today. The web middleware writes the tenant into TenantContext::current(). The report builder calls Request::hasSession() to decide which filters apply: a web export gets a row-visibility filter, a column policy and a redaction pass, and a scheduled export builds its query from the report definition directly. The destination bucket is resolved from the same singleton, in a second place.

What is wrong. First, the tenant for a scheduled export lives in a slot the web middleware also writes, and the queue keeps the container warm between jobs, so a retry can run with a tenant the previous job set. Second, the report builder has to know whether it is running for the web or for a schedule, so every new entry point to a report learns that branch. Third, a scheduled export skips the row filter, the column policy and the audit entry that a web export gets.
blind_pass.pick_why: It puts the split where the paths genuinely differ — how an export starts — so the builder stops asking where it is running, and running both through one filter chain closes the gap. It is the cheapest option that answers all three and far more reversible than extracting a service.
questions: Does any report definition deliberately expose a column the web column policy hides, so that applying it to scheduled exports would change what customers already receive?
Is a missing audit entry for a scheduled export a compliance problem today, or only a gap?
Can two schedules for one tenant run at the same time, or is there at most one export in flight per tenant?
Is the nightly window fixed, or will scheduled exports eventually run on demand from the web as well?
